chunks: PoP thermal behavior. The question: How do PoP chips impact thermals?
In a PoP stack, the memory sits right on top of the processor, which is the hottest chip.
Heat that would have escaped up through the top of the package now has to pass through the memory first.
More heat goes down into the board instead, the processor runs hotter, and the memory gets warmed from below. Memory works worse when it is hot.
Imagine a crowded room with two exit doors, one up and one down. People are the heat. If you narrow the upper door, the crowd backs up, and the room fills more than before.
More people also use the lower door. Adding the memory package narrows the upper door.
The SoC's heat splits between the left (up) branch through the memory package to the case and ambient, and the right (down) branch through the balls into the board.
The memory resistance R mem sits in series on the up path; remove it and the up path falls from 35 to 20 K/W.
Thermal resistance: how many degrees of temperature rise each watt of heat flow causes, in K/W. A lower number is better.
Junction temperature: the temperature of the silicon chip itself. DRAM refresh: memory cells leak their stored charge, so they must be rewritten regularly.
Hotter cells leak faster, so refreshing costs more power and speed. Throttling: the chip slowing itself down to cut heat. PoP: memory stacked on the processor package.
These are round numbers chosen to show the method. A processor's heat has two exits. Down through the board costs 32 K/W. Up through the top costs 20 K/W with no memory.
Because the heat shares two routes, together they act like about 12. 3 K/W. At 3 watts, the chip runs about 3 times 12. 3 = 37 degrees above the surrounding air (ambient).
Add a memory package that costs 15 K/W on the upper route. The top route becomes 35 K/W, and the two routes together act like about 16. 7 K/W.
At 3 watts the chip now runs about 50 degrees above ambient, 13 degrees hotter. That is the whole idea.
"With PoP, the memory sits right on top of the SoC, so heat can't easily go up through the package top; most flows down through the balls into the board, and the DRAM gets heated from below.
As a thermal circuit, an extra 15 K/W in the top path takes the SoC's junction-to-ambient from about 12. 3 to 16. 7 K/W, so at 3 watts the SoC runs about 13 K hotter.
DRAM needs faster refresh above about 85 degrees, so thermals limit PoP to mobile-class power. Fixes: board copper, a spreader over the memory, throttling."
